title: The Miramichi River System, NB
region_name: Southwest & Northwest Miramichi watersheds, central New Brunswick
intro_md:
The Miramichi is New Brunswick's flagship Atlantic salmon river and one of the most storied salmon rivers in the world — a roughly 250 km system draining about 13,000 km², nearly a quarter of the province, through the Southwest Miramichi and Northwest Miramichi branches to a broad estuary at Miramichi Bay. Almost everything in this guide happens well upstream of the city of Miramichi (the amalgamated Newcastle–Chatham–Douglastown–Nelson–Loggieville community at the river mouth), in towns strung along the Southwest branch — Blackville, Doaktown, Boiestown — and along the Northwest branch through Red Bank and Sunny Corner.

The Southwest Miramichi's own major tributaries — the Renous, Dungarvon, Cains, Barnaby and Bartholomew rivers — and the Northwest's Big Sevogle and Little Southwest Miramichi carry salmon, brook trout and, in their lower reaches, striped bass. The Northwest Miramichi estuary is, as far as DFO has been able to confirm, the only successful striped bass spawning ground for the entire southern Gulf of St. Lawrence population — every striper caught from New Brunswick to Nova Scotia to PEI is part of the same stock that spawns here.

**Access is genuinely mixed, and worth understanding before you go.** A public list of named pools exists (see Access, below) and much of the river is fishable water, but the land bordering many pools is privately owned, and the province operates a formal Crown Reserve booking system on top of that for some of the best water. None of this is a formality — showing up without understanding which category the water you're standing in falls into is the single most common way visiting anglers get it wrong here.

**Regulations overview**: Atlantic salmon fishing on the Miramichi falls under DFO Gulf Region, the same regional office as the NB/PEI saltwater guides elsewhere in this app, working alongside New Brunswick's own Fish and Wildlife Branch, which issues licences and manages the Crown Reserve system and Guide Required Waters. A New Brunswick angling licence is required for freshwater species; salmon needs its own salmon licence on top of that. Striped bass, gaspereau, shad and other tidal-water species fall under DFO Gulf Region's own tidal-water rules rather than the provincial book. See each species' own guide for full current details — seasons, limits, closures and Crown Reserve booking windows all change from year to year, sometimes with only days of notice once fish are on the move or water gets warm.

sections.heading: Access: public pools, Crown Reserve, and Guide Required Water
sections.body_md:
**Public pools.** The Miramichi Salmon Association publishes a list of pools it believes are open to public fishing, with coordinates — roughly 18 named pools across the Main Southwest Miramichi (Forks Pool, Dungeon Pool, Gray Rapids, Quarryville, Cache Pool and others near Boiestown), the Cains River, the Dungarvon, the Renous, the Northwest Miramichi and the Little Southwest Miramichi. The MSA is explicit that this is knowledge, not a guarantee: *"When fishing what you believe to be public water, please respect the rights of private property owners. If you see a 'No Fishing' sign or if you are challenged, please leave."* Much of the land bordering these pools is privately owned farmland, and access by long-standing local custom is common — which is also why pool etiquette (arrive at the head, rotate through, don't crowd a pool someone's already fishing) is taken seriously here, more like an unwritten code than a suggestion.

**Crown Reserve water** is the opposite of informal: it's provincially owned angling water booked through a formal system, in three tiers.

- *Regular Crown Reserve* — ten Miramichi-system stretches (on the Little Southwest Miramichi, Lower North Branch, Northwest Miramichi and North Sevogle), booked in 48-hour blocks, June 10–September 15. An annual computer draw allocates most of the season; unsuccessful draw applicants can book from the second Monday of May, and any NB resident can book from the first Monday of June. Anything left unbooked 48 hours out opens to anyone, any residency, first-come. Live release only — 0 retained, max 2 salmon released per angler per day.
- *Daily Crown Reserve* — single-day bookings, June 1–September 15; the Miramichi-system stretch is Cruickshank, on the North Branch Sevogle.
- *Live Release Crown Reserve* — five Miramichi-drainage stretches (the Lower North Branch, Palisades and Sinclair on North Pole Stream, and both the Cains Lower and Cains Upper stretches), fly-only with single barbless or pinched hooks, everything released, June 1–August 31.

Booking and fees run through the NB Department of Natural Resources — the Miramichi office (506-627-4050) handles unclaimed stretches — and every Crown Reserve angler needs the Crown Reserve booking on top of an ordinary salmon licence.

**Guide Required Water** is a separate, broader designation: non-residents must be accompanied by a licensed guide to fish for *any* species on these stretches after a set date each year, typically April 15. It covers most of the system's better-known salmon water — the Main Southwest Miramichi above the Renous confluence, the Little Southwest Miramichi, the Northwest Miramichi above Scott's Rapid Pool, the Cains, Dungarvon, Renous and several smaller tributaries. Two guide types exist: a paid Guide I (professional, up to three waders or one boat angler, can't fish alongside clients but may hook a fish on their behalf), and an unpaid Guide II (an NB resident guiding one non-resident friend or relative, who may fish alongside them). Tidal water and Fish NB Days are exempt from the guide requirement. In practice, a non-resident angling for salmon here should assume a guide is needed unless they've specifically confirmed otherwise for the stretch they're on.

One stretch runs looser than the rest: the Miramichi main stem from the Centennial Bridge (in the city of Miramichi) upstream to Doyle's Brook on the Southwest branch and to the Red Bank/Sunny Corner bridge on the Northwest branch allows barbless single-hook bait or unbaited lures alongside fly — spin gear that's flatly illegal on the fly-only water upstream.

sections.heading: Atlantic Salmon
sections.body_md:
**Why people come here.** The Miramichi is the reason "Maritime salmon fishing" and "the Miramichi" are close to synonyms for a lot of anglers. It's also a river in real, DFO-documented decline: adult returns to the system peaked around 130,000 fish in 1986 and had fallen below 20,000 by 2019, a 68% drop over just the most recent three-generation window assessed (2003–2019) — the lowest on record at the time. That's the context every rule below exists inside. Catch-and-release has been mandatory here since 2015, and DFO reconfirms it every season.

**Season, by stretch (2026, catch-and-release throughout).** The pattern is a spring kelt season (April 15–May 15) then a bright-salmon season that mostly runs May 16–October 15, with real variation: the Northwest Miramichi above Little River and its South Branch have no spring season and a shorter, later bright window (June 10 onward, the South Branch closing August 31); the Bartibog runs bright fish all the way to October 29, the longest window on the system; several tributaries close their bright season a month early, September 15 rather than October 15. Don't assume one date applies system-wide — check the stretch.

**Daily limits, hook-and-release.** Spring kelt: 5 per day. Bright salmon the rest of the season: 2 per day on the Miramichi and Restigouche specifically — lower than the 4 per day allowed on other open NB rivers.

**Gear.** Barbless artificial fly, system-wide, no exceptions for salmon. A long list of specific stretches (Little Southwest Miramichi, Burnthill Brook, Cains below Beaver Brook, Rocky Brook and others) go further and require fly-only gear for *every* species, not just salmon.

**Warm water protocol.** The Miramichi is one of four Gulf-region rivers (with the Restigouche, Nepisiguit and Nova Scotia's Margaree) with a formal warm-water closure mechanism: DFO tracks water temperature and closes water — first a published list of cold-water refuge pools and tributary mouths, then wider stretches if conditions don't improve — when thresholds are crossed, in coordination with the province and local groups. Exact trigger temperatures aren't published, and closures are announced in-season as variation orders rather than fixed dates. Three pools (Sutherland Brook, Wilson Brook and Quarryville/Indiantown Brook) close automatically every year from July 1 to December 31 regardless of temperature. Check DFO's Gulf Region salmon notices before a summer trip — a closure can appear with days of notice.

**Fees and licensing (2026).** Residents: $36/season (ages 16–64) or $20/season (10–15 and 65+). Non-residents: $173/season, $100 for seven days, $53 for three days. Everyone needs a salmon licence on top of a base angling licence to fish for salmon specifically, and stubs must be returned within seven days of the close of the season you fished — even to report you caught nothing — or you risk a fine or losing future privileges.

sections.heading: Striped Bass
sections.body_md:
**The one river this all comes back to.** The Northwest Miramichi estuary is the confirmed spawning ground for the entire southern Gulf striped bass population — not just a good local spot, the source. DFO closes a defined stretch of the estuary (from the Red Bank–Sunny Corner bridge downriver roughly 10 km) for up to ten days once large spawning concentrations show up, typically late May into mid-June, announced as a variation order rather than a fixed annual date. The spawning stock has recovered enormously from under 5,000 fish in the late 1990s to an estimated 547,300 in 2025 (up from 340,300 the year before), which is also reshaping the river's ecology — that same rebound is a documented factor in poor Atlantic salmon smolt survival on this system.

**Regulations (2026, DFO Gulf Region).** Tidal waters: April 15–October 31. On the Miramichi specifically, inland waters run a touch longer, to October 15. Bag and possession limit 4 fish per day, retained within a 50–65 cm slot. Barbless single hooks required everywhere; gear caps at five lines/six hooks per line in tidal water, one line/three hooks inland. Fishing hours shift through the season, and — worth knowing if you're above the city — Miramichi tidal water upstream of the Centennial Bridge follows the tighter sunrise-to-sunset inland-water hours year-round rather than the extended tidal-water hours used downstream.

This is a retention fishery, not catch-and-release like salmon — a real contrast on the same river.

sections.heading: Brook Trout
sections.body_md:
**Season and limits.** Rivers, brooks and streams: May 1–September 15, 5 per day, 10 cm minimum. Lakes, ponds and reservoirs: May 15–September 15, 2 per day over 30 cm. A number of specific stretches — including the Adams Pool Crown Reserve water and several Little Southwest and Northwest Miramichi tributaries — reduce this further, to mandatory release or fly-only.

**Sea-run fish** push into the lower system in spring, typically strongest through May and into June, before the push tapers off through summer — the same window several outfitters describe as prime for fishing the Cains and the main Miramichi together for trout ahead of the bigger salmon season.

sections.heading: Smallmouth Bass — an invasive species here, not a target
sections.body_md:
Smallmouth bass were illegally introduced into Miramichi Lake in 2008 and have since spread into the Southwest Miramichi River itself — they are not native to this system and compete directly with salmon and trout. A rotenone-based eradication effort has targeted the lake and stretches of the river; its status has changed repeatedly and this guide can't promise it's current.

**What actually matters for anyone fishing here**: as of April 1, 2026, New Brunswick added a mandatory-retention condition to angling licences for five invasive species — including smallmouth bass — in river systems where they aren't established, and the Miramichi is explicitly named. If you catch one here, the rule is the reverse of everywhere else in this app: kill and retain it, don't release it.

sources.label: CBC — Invasive smallmouth bass threaten wild Atlantic salmon

sections.heading: American Shad and Gaspereau
sections.body_md:
**Shad**: open year-round in tidal water, 5 fish daily bag and possession limit, no size limit. A June run into the estuary and lower system is popular with fly anglers locally, though the specifics of where and how are colour from outfitters rather than anything DFO documents in detail.

**Gaspereau** (alewife and blueback herring) are managed federally with details set by DFO's Orders Registry rather than fixed in the provincial book, so check current notices rather than assuming a number. The Miramichi's gaspereau stock hasn't been formally sampled since 2000; index-trapnet catches have declined on the Southwest branch and been inconsistent on the Northwest branch since, which is worth knowing if a run feels thinner than its reputation suggests.

sources.label: DFO — Assessment of Gaspereau Stocks, Southern Gulf of St. Lawrence (CSAS Research Doc 2024/041)

spots.name: Forks Pool
spots.description: Where the North and South Branches of the Southwest Miramichi meet near Juniper — the reference point the regulations book itself uses to define the Main Southwest Miramichi. A public pool per the Miramichi Salmon Association's list.

spots.name: Doaktown
spots.description: On the Main Southwest Miramichi, nicknamed the heart of the river valley and home to the Atlantic Salmon Museum — a good base for the middle stretches of the system.

spots.name: Blackville
spots.description: On the Southwest Miramichi, roughly 40 km from the city — central to much of the public-pool and Crown Reserve water on this branch.

spots.name: Boiestown
spots.description: Southwest Miramichi, about 60 km northeast of Fredericton. Cache Pool and Burntland Brook, both on the public pools list, sit nearby.

spots.name: Red Bank / Sunny Corner
spots.description: On the Northwest Miramichi, the bridge here is a recurring regulatory landmark — it marks where fly-only water gives way to the looser gear rules downstream, and where striped bass fishing hours switch to the tighter inland-water rule.

spots.name: Ritchie Wharf Park
spots.description: Public wharf and park in the city of Miramichi, on the Newcastle side — the most clearly documented public access point near the river mouth and estuary.
